headline: Digital India BHASHINI Division Organises Workshop at Maharashtra Mantralaya; Advances Multilingual AI for Inclusive Digital Governance
fullText:
Ministry of Electronics & IT

Digital India BHASHINI Division Organises Workshop at Maharashtra Mantralaya; Advances Multilingual AI for Inclusive Digital Governance

Engagement with Maharashtra’s Language Department Explores the Potential of Language AI to Strengthen Access to Digital Services in Marathi and Other Indian Languages

10 SEP 2026 12:51PM by PIB Delhi

The Digital India BHASHINI Division (DIBD), under the Digital India Corporation (DIC), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, organised a workshop at Maharashtra Mantralaya in collaboration with the Language Department, Government of Maharashtra, to explore the potential of multilingual and voice-enabled Artificial Intelligence (AI) in strengthening access to digital services, government information and citizen-facing applications in preferred languages.

The engagement focused on the role of Language AI in enabling more inclusive, accessible and citizen-centric digital governance, particularly by bringing language technologies closer to citizens in Marathi and other Indian languages. The discussions highlighted the importance of building digital systems that can understand, process and communicate in the languages people use in their everyday lives.

The BHASHINI team showcased its multilingual AI capabilities through live demonstrations of speech recognition, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, translation and voice-enabled interaction. The demonstrations highlighted how these technologies can be integrated into public services to enable more natural and inclusive interaction between citizens and digital systems.

A key focus of the workshop was the importance of high-quality and representative language data in developing locally relevant AI systems. The discussions highlighted opportunities for greater participation by language experts, government institutions, academia and communities in strengthening language datasets and advancing Language AI for Marathi and other Indian languages. In this context, BhashaDaan, BHASHINI’s crowdsourcing initiative, offers a platform for citizens to contribute language data and help build stronger language resources.

The engagement also explored the potential for department-specific Language AI, including the incorporation of specialised terminology used across government departments. Such capabilities can help improve the understanding and processing of government content while enabling more effective multilingual communication across public services.

Discussions further explored the potential of a Maharashtra-focused multilingual AI ecosystem, including the proposed MahaBHASHINI concept, to support language-inclusive experiences across areas such as tourism, transport and other public-facing services. The workshop also provided an opportunity to identify priority use cases and areas for collaboration between the Government of Maharashtra and BHASHINI.

The workshop brought together government officials, language experts and stakeholders to exchange ideas and identify opportunities for collaboration in language technology, datasets, research and real-world applications of Language AI.

The engagement at Maharashtra Mantralaya marks another step towards strengthening Centre-State collaboration in building an inclusive multilingual digital ecosystem, where language becomes an enabler of access, participation and digital empowerment.

About Digital India BHASHINI Division (DIBD)

The Digital India BHASHINI Division (DIBD), under the Digital India Corporation (DIC), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), is building a national ecosystem for AI-powered multilingual digital inclusion. BHASHINI supports 36 Indian text languages, 23 Indian voice languages and 35 international languages, powers 800+ government websites, has enabled 9 billion+ cumulative AI inferences and processes 24 million+ AI inferences daily, helping make Digital Public Infrastructure more accessible through Language AI. National Hub for Language Technology (NHLT) is one of the largest inferencing platforms in the Global South, supporting the growing adoption of Language AI across government and public-facing digital services.

headline: BRICS
fullText:
PIB Backgrounder

Evolution, Cooperation and India's Leadership

10 SEP 2026 12:43PM by PIB Delhi

A boardroom acronym for four emerging markets has grown into something far bigger. Today It is a geopolitical bloc spanning four continents. The journey runs from a four-country dialogue to today's far wider grouping. Successive waves of membership pulled in oil states, African economies and Southeast Asian partners. At the centre of this expanding architecture sits India this year, chairing the grouping for a fourth time since its inception.

BRICS: Shaping an Inclusive Global Order

BRICS has emerged as a key platform for coordinating economic policy among major emerging economies. It serves as the principal forum where these nations shape a common position on global governance. Through sustained dialogue, it has become a channel for advancing the interests of the Global South within multilateral institutions. Its agenda spans development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges. The grouping reflects the growing economic weight and aspirations of emerging economies globally. It provides members with a platform to share experiences and address common challenges.

Under its 2026 Presidency, India is set to host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026. It will mark India’s fourth Chairship of BRICS in 2026. India’s Chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” The theme reflects India’s focus on strengthening existing achievements and institutional effectiveness. It places development, sustainability and innovation at the heart of the agenda. It also highlights the aspirations of the Global South. India seeks to reinforce BRICS as a constructive and solutions-oriented forum.

Today, BRICS comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE. Collectively, these members represent 49.5% of the global population, 40% of global GDP, and 26% of global trade. These figures underline their substantial demographic and economic weight. Its expanded membership has also widened its geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. This diversity brings together major markets, natural resources, technological capabilities and varied development experiences.

The Origin The acronym ‘BRIC’ was coined in 2001 by Goldman Sachs in its Global Economics Paper, ‘The World Needs Better Economic BRICs.’ Based on econometric analysis, the paper projected that Brazil, Russia, India and China would be among the world’s largest economies over the following five decades. Their growing economic weight and vast geographic reach across three continents highlighted their emerging global significance. The BRIC concept subsequently evolved into a formal grouping, with South Africa joining in 2010 and transforming BRIC into BRICS. The evolution marked the transition from an economic grouping identified by analysts to a formal platform for political, economic and development cooperation.

The Aim, Objective and Areas of Cooperation

BRICS was initially conceived as a forum for dialogue on major issues shaping the international agenda. Its early focus was on developing common positions on global political and economic matters. It sought to promote a more democratic, legitimate and balanced international order. The grouping also emphasised sustainable economic and social development, social inclusion and shared prosperity among emerging economies. Over time, these priorities have provided a foundation for deeper and broader engagement among members.

Across successive summits, BRICS cooperation has progressively expanded to encompass strategic global issues and areas of practical collaboration. Its agenda covers terrorism, climate change, food and energy security, trade and agriculture. It also addresses labour and employment, telecommunications, international finance and the global economic situation. BRICS advocates for greater representation and equity in international institutions, including the WTO and global financial architecture. These efforts seek to make global governance more inclusive, effective and responsive to contemporary challenges.

BRICS Through the Years: From Crisis to Collective Action

The 2008 global financial crisis marked a defining moment in the evolution of BRICS. It exposed gaps in the existing global financial architecture. It also created a need for broader consensus on global economic governance. The four BRIC countries articulated a common position on these issues. They called for a more representative international financial system. They sought greater voice for emerging economies in the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. They also opposed protectionism and supported an open, rules-based multilateral trading system. This coordination laid the foundation for the first BRIC Summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009.

BRIC was formally established in 2006 as a political cooperation forum among Brazil, Russia, India and China. Its founding members shared an aspiration for a more representative and equitable global order. South Africa joined as a full member in 2011, transforming BRIC into BRICS. This inclusion expanded the grouping’s geographical representation across continents. The grouping subsequently broadened its agenda beyond economic issues to development, finance, health, climate action, technology and trade. This evolution strengthened BRICS as a wider framework for engagement among emerging economies.

A Wider BRICS: Expanding Reach, Deepening Engagement

A major phase of expansion began in January 2024. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE became full members. Indonesia joined as the eleventh full member in January 2025. These accessions significantly expanded BRICS’ geographical and economic reach. The expansion was accompanied by the creation of a Partner Country category. Ten countries joined this framework during 2025: Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam. The new arrangement provides an additional channel for structured engagement with BRICS.

The Partner Country framework broadens BRICS’ outreach without altering its full-membership structure. It strengthens opportunities for South-South cooperation across Asia, Africa, Latin America and Eurasia. The wider network also creates scope for collaboration on trade, finance, climate action and sustainable development. It reflects growing interest among emerging economies in participating in discussions on global governance.

The evolution of BRICS demonstrates a shift from a four-country economic dialogue to a broader framework for political, economic, financial and social cooperation. Its expansion has increased its demographic and economic weight. It has also broadened its regional representation and areas of engagement. The grouping’s institutional evolution has kept pace with the changing priorities of emerging economies.

BRICS Presidency: Rotation and Responsibilities The BRICS Presidency rotates annually according to the letters of its acronym. Each Presidency term begins on January 1st and concludes on December 31st of the respective year. The country holding the Presidency sets the priorities of the agenda for that year. It also organizes the group's annual Summit and steers key ministerial and working group meetings. With the recent expansion of BRICS membership, a new rotation formula for the Presidency is also being discussed among member countries.

India at the Helm of BRICS: From Continuity to Consensus

Before this year, India has previously chaired BRICS in 2012, 2016 and 2021. Each Chairship reflected the priorities and challenges of its respective period. India’s repeated leadership demonstrates its sustained engagement with the grouping. It also reflects India’s commitment to constructive multilateralism and the priorities of developing economies.

2012: Laying the Foundation for Stronger Cooperation

India hosted the Fourth BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 29 March 2012. The Summit was held under the theme “BRICS Partnership for Global Stability, Security and Prosperity.” Discussions focused on global governance reform, sustainable development, food security and energy security. The Summit adopted the Delhi Declaration and an Action Plan for strengthening BRICS cooperation. The outcomes established a stronger foundation for institutional and sectoral engagement. Click to Read More About the Delhi Declaration

Major Outcomes The Summit proposed exploring a new Development Bank to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable development projects. The proposed institution would serve BRICS, emerging economies and developing countries. It would complement existing multilateral and regional financial institutions in supporting global growth and development. Click to Read More About the NDB. Member nations signed the Master Agreement on Extending Credit Facility in Local Currency and boost intra-BRICS trade. The summit also laid the foundation for the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA) as a financial safety mechanism for BRICS countries. The arrangement was designed to provide short-term liquidity support and help member countries address financial instability. India institutionalized new joint tracks for practical cooperation in agriculture, health, and science.

2016: Goa Summit Expanded BRICS Outreach

India hosted the Eighth BRICS Summit in Goa in October 2016. The Summit was held under the theme “Building Responsive, Inclusive and Collective Solutions.” India’s Chairship focused on strengthening intra-BRICS cooperation and expanding outreach. It also advanced collaboration on counter-terrorism, trade, innovation and multilateral coordination. The Goa Summit reinforced the grouping’s focus on emerging global challenges and practical cooperation.

Major Outcome The operationalization of the New Development Bank was solidified with the rollout of its first set of financial loans, primarily backing renewable energy projects. BRICS elevated renewable energy access, clean energy transition and energy security as shared priorities. Greater focus was placed on combating HIV and tuberculosis. India secured stronger BRICS language on combating terrorism and called for adherence to FATF (Financial Action Task Force) standards. The Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) Outreach Summit expanded engagement between BRICS and countries of the wider Bay of Bengal region. Discussions covered counter-terrorism, trade, energy, investment, environment, technology and infrastructure. Agreement to establish BRICS Agriculture Research Platform, BRICS Railway Research Network, BRICS Sports Council and various youth-centric cooperation forums.

2021: Consolidating Cooperation in a Changing World

India hosted the 13th BRICS Summit virtually on 9 September 2021. The Summit marked the 15th anniversary of BRICS. It was held under the theme “BRICS@15: Intra-BRICS Cooperation for Continuity, Consolidation and Consensus.” India focused on strengthening institutional continuity, deepening cooperation and building greater consensus. The Chairship also advanced cooperation across health, digital technologies, counter-terrorism and sustainable development.

Major Outcomes India led the adoption of a unified BRICS Counter-Terrorism Action Plan. Click to Read More about Action Plan. India hosted the first-ever BRICS Digital Health Summit during its Chairship. A BRICS Vaccine Research and Development Center was launched to collectively address current and future pandemic responses. Agreement on Cooperation for the BRICS Remote Sensing Satellite Constellation. it enables countries to share remote-sensing data for environmental protection, disaster management, and climate monitoring. India introduced new ministerial-level working paths, launching the BRICS Alliance for Green Tourism and the first BRICS Water Ministers Meeting for sustainable resource management.

Through successive Chairships, India has contributed to the institutional and substantive development of BRICS. Its priorities have evolved with emerging global challenges while retaining a focus on practical cooperation. India’s 2026 Chairship builds on this experience and the grouping’s expanded membership.

BRICS 2026: Key Outcomes Emerging from Ministerial Meetings

India assumed its fourth BRICS Chairship on 1 January 2026. During its Chairship, India convened a series of ministerial meetings across priority areas of BRICS cooperation. Over the year, BRICS members countries exchanged views on shared priorities and global and regional developments. These discussions advanced cooperation across the grouping’s three fundamental pillars. The pillars comprise political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.

More than 350 meetings and high-level engagements were held across 25 cities during India’s Chairship. The meetings generated practical and development-oriented outcomes across key areas of cooperation. The following outcomes emerged from ministerial meetings held during India’s 2026 BRICS Chairship.

BRICS Centres of Excellence on Agro-Ecology agreed upon as a collaborative platform for joint research, knowledge sharing and capacity building on natural, organic and regenerative farming practices to promote climate-resilient and sustainable agricultural systems (initially coordinated by ICAR-Indian Institute of Farming Systems Research, Modipuram). BRICS Network on Digital Agriculture to deepen cooperation and scale the deployment of AI‑driven decision‑support systems, geospatial intelligence, IoT‑enabled monitoring, and advanced data analytics in agriculture (initially coordinated by IIT Delhi).

BRICS AGRIN (Agro-Inputs, Genetic Resources and Information Network) agreed upon as a voluntary, farmer-centric cooperation framework among BRICS countries to strengthen collaboration in seeds, germplasm, and agricultural inputs.

BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle: The priority was launched along with the BRICS Roadmap for a Joint Initiative on Healthy Lifestyle Promotion (2026-2029). It aims to serve as a collaborative platform for technical cooperation, knowledge exchange and coordinated awareness initiatives, promoting preventive and life-course approaches to obesity and other non-communicable diseases.

BRICS Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCIM): It aims to serve as a platform for structured and consensus-based cooperation on TCIM, covering policy dialogue, research and evidence generation, capacity building and academic exchange, digital knowledge platforms, quality and regulatory standards, and the protection of traditional and indigenous knowledge.

Focus on Mental Health through BRICS Training Hub Network and BRICS Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India as the coordinating Centre. It aims to optimize human resources for mental health through upskilling, task-sharing and standardized training, and to integrate mental well-being into primary healthcare.

Mainstreaming Traditional Knowledge through adoption of BRICS Principles for Advancing Climate Resilience through People-centric and Community-based Adaptation and BRICS Guiding Principles on Strengthening Academic Collaboration on Traditional and Indigenous Knowledge Systems.

Advancing Sustainable Lifestyles through Network of BRICS Institutions to Advance Knowledge Sharing, Research & Innovation and Sustainable Lifestyles Week for exchange of knowledge on policies, programmes, initiatives and leading practices; conduct capacity-building workshops on thematic areas; facilitate dialogue among stakeholders including academic and research institutions; and compilation of case studies.

BRICS CONNECT for Skilling: A BRICS Cooperation Network for Capacity Building, Employability, and New Skills and Technologies (BRICS CONNECT), building on the BRICS Virtual Liaison Office. It is a flexible platform with four components, namely capacity building for advancing social security, women’s participation in the workforce, skills and employability, and digital public infrastructure. Cooperation under it is voluntary and non-binding.

Smart Grids and Energy Storage: The BRICS Guiding Principles on Energy Storage and Smart Grids were adopted and the BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage was launched to serve as a voluntary platform for knowledge sharing, capacity building, the exchange of policy and regulatory best practices, and promotion of pilot initiatives among BRICS countries.

Urban Infrastructure strengthened through establishment of BRICS Urban Mobility Hub, a virtual collaborative platform which will promote knowledge sharing, capacity building and technical cooperation in sustainable urban mobility; adoption of BRICS Voluntary Principles for Climate Resilient Urban Infrastructure to support the integration of climate and disaster risk considerations into urban planning, design, investment, construction, and maintenance; and establishment of a BRICS Urban Research and Knowledge Network for applied urban research, cross-border peer learning, and sustained institutional collaboration.

BRICS MSME Cooperation Portal, to serve as a digital ecosystem accessible to all BRICS member countries, supporting MSMEs, technology centers and clusters, trade associations, financial institutions, training and capacity-building institutions, policymakers, and other relevant stakeholders, along with an institutionalized Dialogue on MSME Finance and Workplan on the Internationalisation of MSMEs were key outcomes to leverage BRICS for enhancing MSMEs’ access to markets and finance.

BRICS Incubator Network, a digital interface/network to connect National Nodal Agencies, selected incubators and start-ups across BRICS countries, facilitate registration and linkages with participating incubators, and enable referral of qualified start-ups to incubators in other BRICS countries.

BRICS Startup Innovation Fund to catalyse financing for early and growth stage startups and foster innovation driven entrepreneurship in BRICS countries.

BRICS Science and Research Repository welcomed as a structured platform for scientific knowledge storage and sharing among BRICS countries.

BRICS Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework: A voluntary, consensus-based framework to strengthen cross-sector transport logistics resilience and sustainability. It aims to address fragmented supply chains and weak connectivity by promoting technical exchange, knowledge sharing on cargo and shipping services, localized assembly and manufacturing ecosystems, and capacity building, while advancing environmentally sustainable and climate-resilient logistics practices.

BRICS Cooperation on Global Value Chains through GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and GVC Joint Study for enhanced BRICS cooperation to ensure that GVCs are resilient, efficient and productive; and to advance the opening of markets and economic diversification among BRICS Members.

BRICS Agreement on Cooperation and Mutual Administrative Assistance in Customs Matters: Members confirmed their in-principle approval and willingness to sign the Agreement to support faster trade, lower transaction costs, more secure borders, trusted trade facilitation, improved ease of doing business, and tackling illicit trade.

Cooperation in the Field of Standardization through an MoU signed by BRICS National Standards Body Heads, a formal framework to strengthen collaboration in the development, adoption and implementation of standards, promote information sharing, exchange of best practices, technical cooperation and capacity building, reinforce quality infrastructure, enhance consumer protection, reduce technical barriers to trade.

BRICS Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 adopted as a reference document to support continuity, coherence and structured cooperation to guide future dialogue, experience sharing and the consideration of practical initiatives under the BRICS Youth Track.

Sport Technology Cooperation institutionalized through a new Working Group to promote cooperation in the field of sport technology in the form of exchange of good practices, institutional experiences, technical information and research inputs.

The ministerial meeting outcomes under India’s 2026 BRICS Chairship reflect a continued focus on practical cooperation, inclusive growth and a stronger voice for the Global South.

2026: Steering BRICS Towards a More Inclusive Future

India’s 2026 BRICS Chairship comes at a time of significant global transformation. The international system is experiencing economic fragmentation, technological disruption and geopolitical uncertainty. Climate change and resource pressures are adding further complexity. These interconnected challenges require cooperation that is inclusive, practical and responsive to diverse national circumstances.

BRICS provides an important avenue for addressing these challenges through dialogue and coordinated action. Its expanded membership brings diverse perspectives from major emerging economies. The grouping can help advance cooperation on development, climate action, technology, energy and financial resilience. It can also contribute to discussions on reforms in global institutions.

For India, the objective extends beyond expanding the grouping’s scale. It is about converting greater representation into meaningful cooperation and tangible outcomes. India’s Chairship seeks to build consensus across diverse members while strengthening the effectiveness of existing mechanisms. India aims to reinforce BRICS as a constructive force for a more inclusive global order.

headline: NIELIT Digital University (NDU) Platform Integrated with Saylor University, USA
fullText:
Ministry of Electronics & IT

NIELIT Digital University (NDU) Platform Integrated with Saylor University, USA

Shri S. Krishnan, Secretary, MeitY Launched the NDU Platform-Saylor University Collaboration; NIELIT also Exchanged MoUs with various Association, Industry and Academia Partners

10 SEP 2026 12:29PM by PIB Delhi

The National Institute of Electronics & Information Technology (NIELIT), under the Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology (MeitY), launched a collaboration with Saylor University, USA to integrate Saylor’s digital learning resources into the NIELIT Digital University (NDU) platform.

Shri S. Krishnan, Secretary, MeitY, attended as Chief Guest and formally inaugurated the partnership. The event took place at the MeitY, New Delhi.

Through this integration, learners on the NDU platform will gain access to a wider range of quality, self-paced and globally relevant online courses and learning resources offered by Saylor University. The initiative is expected to provide learners with greater flexibility and choice in pursuing digital learning, while creating a unified ecosystem that brings together national and international learning opportunities on a common platform.

The collaboration marks an important step towards strengthening India's digital learning ecosystem through international academic partnership and technology-enabled education. It is expected to further enhance the reach and utility of the NIELIT Digital University (NDU) platform, particularly by facilitating wider access to digital education and supporting learners in acquiring contemporary knowledge and skills relevant to the evolving technology and employment landscape. The initiative also reflects NIELIT's commitment to leveraging global partnerships to expand opportunities for lifelong learning, digital upskilling and skill development.

Shri S Krishnan, Secretary, MeitY, who graced the event as the Chief Guest, congratulated NIELIT on the launch of the collaboration between the NIELIT Digital University Platform and Saylor University, USA. He appreciated the initiative as an important step towards expanding access to quality digital learning and strengthening opportunities for skilling, upskilling and lifelong learning. He highlighted the significance of such global collaborations in enhancing the digital education ecosystem and preparing learners with relevant skills to meet the evolving requirements of the technology-driven economy.

He also congratulated all stakeholders on the exchange of MoUs with leading organisations, including the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), NASSCOM, Electronics Sector Skills Council of India (ESSCI), Pearson India Education Services Pvt. Ltd., Stemlore Innovators LLP, Dassault Systèmes, ABES Engineering College, and Kavayitri Bahinabai Chaudhari North Maharashtra University (KBCNMU), Jalgaon. He described these collaborations as significant steps towards strengthening India’s digital skilling and education ecosystem, fostering stronger industry–academia linkages, and expanding access to quality, technology-enabled and industry-relevant learning opportunities.

Shri Krishnan emphasised the need to align skilling and talent development with the evolving requirements of industry and the global digital economy and highlighted the importance of continuous learning, upskilling and reskilling to ensure that India’s talent pool remains relevant and competitive.

Delivering his opening remarks, Dr. M. M. Tripathi, Director General, NIELIT, welcomed the distinguished guests and partner organisations and emphasised the importance of partnerships in strengthening digital education, skilling and emerging technology capabilities, while expanding access to quality, flexible and industry-relevant learning opportunities.

Dr. Tripathi highlighted that the collaboration will further enrich the digital learning ecosystem, facilitate continuous upskilling and reskilling, and create greater opportunities for learners to acquire relevant skills in line with the evolving requirements of the digital economy. He also underscored the role of such initiatives in supporting the development of a future-ready and globally competitive workforce.

Dr. David Shulman, Provost and Senior Vice President, Saylor University, USA, welcomed the collaboration and highlighted its potential to expand access to quality, flexible and industry-relevant digital education. Dr. Shulman emphasised the role of the NIELIT Digital University (NDU) Platform in providing learners with a flexible digital learning environment and noted that integration of Saylor University’s free, self-paced online courses in areas such as AI, programming, data science, cybersecurity and business management would further enrich the NDU learning ecosystem.

He stated that combining NIELIT’s nationwide digital reach with Saylor University’s open-learning resources through the NDU Platform can expand learning opportunities for students, working professionals and learners seeking to upskill or reskill, while contributing to a digitally skilled and globally competitive workforce, including in Tier-2, Tier-3 and underserved regions.

Delivering the keynote address, Dr. Sheila Jagannathan, Vice President, Saylor University, USA, emphasised that rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence and other emerging technologies require a skilled workforce committed to continuous learning and upskilling.

Dr. Jagannathan highlighted the potential of the NIELIT Digital University (NDU) Platform to provide flexible, self-paced learning pathways and credentials. She noted that Saylor University offers more than 160+ free online courses in areas including AI, data science, programming and cybersecurity. She stated that the collaboration brings together NIELIT’s nationwide reach and Saylor University’s open-learning resources to democratise access to education, enhance employability and support the development of a future-ready and globally competitive workforce.

Delivering the closing remarks, Dr. Alok Tripathi, Director (Scheme/Skilling) & Chief Controller of Examinations, NIELIT, highlighted that these partnerships would further strengthen NIELIT’s efforts towards digital skilling, emerging technologies and industry-oriented learning, while creating wider opportunities for learners across the country. He expressed appreciation to all stakeholders for their continued support and concluded the event with a call for sustained collaboration towards building a future-ready and globally competitive digital workforce.

Exchange of MoUs with Partner Organisations

As part of the event, NIELIT exchanged Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with 08 partner organisations from association, industry and academia. The collaborations are aimed at expanding industry-aligned skilling, certification, faculty development, internships and digital learning opportunities, largely leveraging the NDU platform. The partner organisations are:

Confederation of Indian Industry (CII)

National Association of Software and Services Companies (NASSCOM)

Electronics Sector Skills Council of India (ESSCI)

Pearson India Education Services Pvt. Ltd.

STEM Learning and Outreach for Research and Education (STEMLORE)

Dassault Systèmes

ABES Engineering College

Kavayitri Bahinabai Chaudhari North Maharashtra University (KBCNMU), Jalgaon

National Institute of Electronics & Information Technology (NIELIT), an Autonomous Scientific Society of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, has been a pioneer in skill development and digital empowerment.

With its extensive presence through 56 NIELIT centers, over 700 accredited institutes, and 8,000+ facilitation centers, NIELIT has skilled and certified millions of students in emerging technologies in the E&ICT domain.

NIELIT has been conferred the status of "Deemed to be University" under the distinct category as per UGC (Institution Deemed to be Universities) Regulations, 2023 having its main campus at Ropar (Punjab) and eleven constituent campuses located in Aizawl, Agartala, Calicut, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Gorakhpur, Imphal, Itanagar, Ajmer, Kohima, Patna and Srinagar, aims to revolutionize higher education in E&ICT domain using digital technologies.

About NIELIT Digital University (NDU) platform

The NIELIT Digital University (NDU) Platform is a next-generation digital learning ecosystem launched on 2 October 2025 to provide accessible, affordable and industry-aligned education in emerging technologies. With 2.80 lakh+ registered learners, NDU offers 120+ courses across AI, Cyber Security, Data Science, Cloud Computing, Semiconductor Design, VLSI and other frontier domains. Reaching learners across all 36 States/UTs and 761 districts, the platform supports anytime-anywhere online and blended learning through AI-enabled tools, Virtual Labs and an advanced Learning Management System. NDU also offers NSQF-aligned, NCVET-approved programmes, ABC-enabled credit transfer, and personalized learning pathways, strengthening employability and lifelong skill development.

headline: Fueling the Blue Economy
fullText:
PIB Backgrounder

Fueling the Blue Economy

Six Years of Empowering India’s Fisheries Sector under PMMSY

10 SEP 2026 12:25PM by PIB Delhi

The Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) has strengthened India’s fisheries sector. The Government allocated a record ₹2,500 crore in BE 2026–27 under PMMSY, reaffirming its commitment to the sector. Fish production increased from 141.64 lakh tonnes in 2019-20 to a record 197.75 lakh tonnes in 2024-25. Fisheries exports rose from ₹46,663 crore in 2019–20 to ₹73,890 crore in 2025–26, reflecting strong sectoral growth. The scheme created employment opportunities for 58 lakh persons in fisheries and aquaculture-related activities. It also approved ₹2,797 crore for cold-chain and marketing infrastructure, strengthening post-harvest management and market connectivity. Additionally, 2,195 FFPOs were supported through projects worth ₹544.86 crore, strengthening collective empowerment.

Strengthening India’s Blue Economy

India's fisheries sector is a vital economic pillar, sustaining nearly three crore livelihoods, especially among marginalised and coastal communities. As a recognised Sunrise Sector, it has seen consistent growth driven by policies that boost production, exports, infrastructure, and technology adoption. To further unlock this potential, the Government introduced the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY), focused on fostering inclusive and sustainable growth across the sector. As PMMSY completes six years on 10 September 2026, it stands as a landmark in the transformation of the Indian fisheries sector towards modernisation, sustainability, and prosperity. Since its launch in 2020, the scheme has built stronger infrastructure, opened up new opportunities, and provided consistent support to fishers and fish farmers across the country. Building on the Blue Revolution scheme, PMMSY was conceived to address critical gaps across the fisheries value chain.

The Government has been implementing PMMSY since 2020–21, with a total outlay of ₹20,750 crore. The Government reaffirmed its commitment by allocating a record ₹2,500 crore in BE 2026–27 under PMMSY, strengthening fisheries infrastructure and livelihoods. The scheme has also continued to support large-scale investments in fisheries and aquaculture infrastructure. As of 11th August 2026, during the period 2020–21 to 2025–26, the Department of Fisheries has approved fisheries and aquaculture projects worth ₹21,394.88 crore, including a Central share of ₹9,510.89 crore. These approvals, based on proposals received from States, Union Territories and various implementing agencies, are supporting infrastructure development and strengthening the fisheries value chain across the country.

PMMSY has focused on transforming India’s fisheries sector by enhancing production and productivity, modernising the value chain, generating livelihood opportunities, increasing incomes, boosting exports and GVA, strengthening fishers’ security and welfare, and improving fisheries management and regulation.

Success Story: From Ice Plant to Greater Prosperity

In Porbandar, Gujarat, Mr. Pravinbhai Babulal Masani has spent over two decades building his fishing enterprise. With extensive experience in the industry, he understood that investing in a new ice plant could strengthen his business. However, the high cost of establishing an ice plant was beyond his financial capacity. The Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) provided him with an opportunity through financial assistance for establishing ice plants.

In 2021–22, Mr. Masani successfully received a ₹48 lakh subsidy under PMMSY. With this support, he established a 30 MT/day ice plant, enabling him to produce high-quality ice blocks for fishing boats. The new facility helps fishing boats carry sufficient ice to keep fish fresh and reduce spoilage during fishing operations. This has strengthened Mr. Masani’s fishing business, improved his earnings, and supported a better livelihood for his family. His journey demonstrates how targeted support under PMMSY can help fishers invest in essential infrastructure, strengthen their businesses, and contribute to fisheries growth.

Transforming India’s Fisheries Sector through PMMSY

The PMMSY is an umbrella scheme comprising Central Sector (CS) and Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) components.

Central Sector (CS): Fully funded and implemented by the Central Government. The Central Sector component supports genetic improvement, innovation, technology demonstrations, training, aquatic quarantine, harbour modernisation, disease surveillance and fisheries data systems. It also strengthens the National Fisheries Development Board (NFDB) and fisheries institutions, fisher safety, FFPOs, cooperatives and SHGs, while promoting certification, traceability, accreditation and labelling. The Pradhan Mantri Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana (PM-MKSSY) is a Central Sector sub-scheme. It operates under the broader ambit of PMMSY. The scheme complements and reinforces PMMSY's overarching objectives. Its specific mandate is to strengthen the development of the fisheries sector.

Pradhan Mantri Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana (PM-MKSSY)

The Pradhan Mantri Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana (PM-MKSSY) is a Central Sector sub-scheme implemented under the umbrella of the PMMSY. Operational across all States and Union Territories for four years from 2023-24 to 2026-27, it carries an estimated financial outlay of ₹6,000 crore.

The scheme facilitates the structural transformation of the fisheries sector by advancing formalisation, expanding insurance coverage, strengthening access to institutional finance, and promoting quality assurance and traceability across the fisheries value chain. It aims to enhance financial resilience, risk mitigation, and market integration for fishers, aquaculture farmers, and allied stakeholders, thereby fostering a more organised, transparent, and sustainable fisheries sector.

Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS): Partially funded by the Central Government and implemented by States and Union Territories. CSS activities include:

Enhancement of Fish Production and Productivity: Focuses on increasing fish production and productivity through technology infusion and improved fisheries practices. It covers inland fisheries, marine fisheries, mariculture, seaweed cultivation, development of fisheries in Himalayan and North-Eastern States/UTs, and ornamental fisheries.

Infrastructure and Post-Harvest Management: Strengthens fisheries infrastructure through fishing harbours, fish landing centres and post-harvest facilities. It also supports cold-chain infrastructure, deep-sea fishing, integrated modern coastal fishing villages, markets and marketing infrastructure.

Fisheries Management and Regulatory Framework: Promotes monitoring, control and surveillance, insurance for fishing vessels and fishers, and fisheries extension and support services. It also strengthens the safety and security of fishers at sea while supporting the livelihood and nutritional needs of fishers.

PMMSY: Strengthening Production, Infrastructure and Livelihoods

The PMMSY has made significant contributions over the past six years towards increasing fish production, enhancing fisheries exports, and creating livelihoods and employment opportunities.

Fish production increased from 141.64 lakh tonnes in 2019-20 to a record 197.75 lakh tonnes in 2024-25.

--The scheme has created direct and indirect employment opportunities for 58 lakh persons in fisheries and aquaculture-related activities.

Fisheries exports increased from ₹46,663 crore in 2019-20 to ₹73,890 crore in 2025-26.

Expanding Modern Aquaculture and Fisheries Infrastructure

Under PMMSY, 12 Integrated Aquaparks have been approved at a total cost of ₹713.80 crore.

During the last 5 years (2020-25), projects worth ₹198.17 crore have been approved towards seaweed cultivation and its allied activities.

52,058 reservoir cages and 23,285.06 hectares of pond area have been approved for inland aquaculture. The scheme has also supported 12,081 Recirculatory Aquaculture Systems (RAS) and 4,205 Biofloc units.

2,672 ornamental fish rearing and integrated ornamental fish units have been supported under PMMSY.

Strengthening Fisheries Infrastructure and Value Chain

The Government is strengthening fisheries infrastructure under PMMSY, with a focus on fishing harbours, fish landing centres, cold chains, transportation and marketing facilities. During the last five years, the Department of Fisheries has approved ₹3,741.89 crore for 28 fishing harbour development/modernisation projects, 25 fish landing centre projects and 23 dredging projects.

Additionally, ₹2,797 crore has been approved for the development of cold-chain and marketing infrastructure. As of 11th August 2026, the approved projects include:

28,489 fish transportation units

1,394 live fish vending units, 6,018 fish kiosks, 117 retail fish markets

775 cold storage & ice plants and 24 wholesale fish markets.

These interventions are strengthening post-harvest management, cold chains, transportation, and market access for inland fisheries produce.

Empowering Communities through Collective Action, Resilience and Technology

The PMMSY is strengthening fisheries through infrastructure development, community empowerment, climate resilience and technology adoption.

Promoting Collective Empowerment through FFPOs

The Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) provides financial assistance for establishing Fish Farmers Producer Organizations (FFPOs) to economically empower fishers and fish farmers and strengthen their bargaining power. From FY 2021–22 to FY 2025–26, the Department of Fisheries approved projects worth ₹544.86 crore to establish 2,195 FFPOs nationwide, supporting incubation, management costs, and equity grants.

Building Climate-Resilient Coastal Communities

Under PMMSY, the Department of Fisheries has identified 100 coastal fishermen villages as Climate Resilient Coastal Fishermen Villages (CRCFV) to strengthen climate resilience and make them economically vibrant. The initiative is being implemented under the Central Sector component of PMMSY, with a unit cost of ₹200 lakh per village, fully funded by the Government, and supports resilient infrastructure, livelihoods and post-harvest facilities for coastal fishing communities.

Technology-Driven Aquaculture

The scheme promotes technology-driven aquaculture systems that enhance productivity while optimising land and water use. It supports high-density, water-efficient models such as Recirculatory Aquaculture Systems (RAS) and Bio-floc technology, improving output, water quality, resource efficiency and environmental sustainability.

Recirculatory Aquaculture System (RAS): RAS filters and recirculates water, removing waste and impurities while enabling intensive fish farming with minimal land and water.

Bio-floc Technology: It is a sustainable aquaculture method that recycles nutrients in water using beneficial microbes. These microbes form clumps called bio-floc, which serve as natural feed and also help clean the water. This method requires little or no water exchange, making it ideal for high-density fish farming with minimal resources. It boosts productivity while being environmentally friendly, earning it the name “green soup” or heterotrophic ponds in aquaculture circles.

Digital Transformation of Fisheries

Beyond modernising production systems, PMMSY is also driving the digital transformation of the fisheries sector. The National Fisheries Digital Platform (NFDP) was launched under PM-MKSSY in September 2024. It aims to advance digital governance and formalisation in the fisheries and aquaculture sector. The NFDP creates work-based digital identities and a comprehensive stakeholder database to formalise the sector. Operationally, it functions as a single-window digital system, enabling beneficiaries to access institutional credit, aquaculture insurance, traceability mechanisms, and performance-linked incentives. The platform also supports fisheries cooperatives, training, and capacity-building initiatives. As of 8 September 2026, the NFDP platform has recorded over 37.01 lakh individual registrations, with total registrations crossing 37.23 lakh.

Contribution to SDG 14: Life Below Water

PMMSY promotes sustainable and responsible fisheries and aquaculture, supporting the sustainable use of aquatic resources. The scheme also promotes sustainable fish production methods and modern aquaculture practices, including Bio-floc, RAS, cage culture and mariculture. These interventions contribute to SDG 14 (Life Below Water) by supporting sustainable management of fisheries and aquaculture and strengthening aquatic resource conservation.

Towards Sustainable Fisheries and Blue Economy Growth

The fisheries sector occupies an important place in India’s agricultural and rural economy, contributing to livelihoods, food security, employment and exports. The Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) is driving the transformation of India’s fisheries sector by strengthening production, infrastructure, technology, livelihoods and sustainability. Its investments in modern infrastructure, cold-chain facilities, technology-driven aquaculture and digital platforms are strengthening the fisheries value chain. Continued support for fishers, fish farmers and coastal communities can create opportunities for higher incomes and improved market access. These efforts also contribute to Sustainable Development Goal 14 (Life Below Water) by promoting sustainable use and conservation of aquatic resources. With sustained investments, PMMSY has laid the foundation for a modern, competitive and sustainable fisheries sector. As India advances its Blue Economy vision, PMMSY will continue to play a pivotal role in enhancing livelihoods, strengthening food security, boosting exports and promoting responsible utilisation of aquatic resources.

headline: Shri. Rajiv Gauba Calls for Deregulation as the Defining Feature of India's Next-Generation Reforms at Global Fintech Fest 2026
fullText:
Shri. Rajiv Gauba Calls for Deregulation as the Defining Feature of India's Next-Generation Reforms at Global Fintech Fest 2026

10 SEP 2026 12:08PM by PIB Delhi

Shri Rajiv Gauba, Member, NITI Aayog, participated in a fireside chat on "From Regulation to Transformation: Building India's Next-Generation Reform Architecture" at the Global Fintech Fest 2026, a conversation spanning India's regulatory journey, the need for balance between innovation and oversight in fintech, and the institutional changes needed to sustain growth to achieve the Viksit Bharat vision.

Reflecting on the reforms of the past decade, Shri Gauba noted that measures such as the Goods and Services Tax, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and a liberalized foreign investment regime had reshaped the economy and opened up sectors once considered off-limits to private enterprise, including defence, space and now nuclear energy.

He said the next-generation reform architecture should be defined by “deregulation”, with the focus on “nuts-and-bolts” reform, on doing away with the license – approval –permission and frequent renewals regime that prevails in different avatars. He emphasised the need to systematically review laws, regulations and administrative processes. This work, he said, is being carried out by a High-Level Committee, guided by the philosophy of Trust Based Governance espoused by the Prime Minister.

Many important reforms, he noted, fall in the domain of States and municipal governments and pointed to the work being done by the Deregulation Task Force, carrying the Trust-Based Governance principles down to the State and city level. Citing the scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment and the Urban Challenge Fund, he characterized the Center Governments approach as "cooperative federalism with a competitive edge", where scheme incentives are linked to reform milestones and projects are selected through challenge mode.

On fintech, Shri Gauba highlighted India’s phenomenal growth in the sector and how it has contributed to financial inclusion and access. He cited India's digital public infrastructure - from Aadhaar and UPI to DigiLocker and the account aggregator framework – as a model that the world can replicate, where Governments lays open, secure and interoperable rails on which private enterprise builds and innovates. He said regulation in technology-driven sectors should strike a dynamic balance between protecting public interest and allowing innovation to flourish. Regulatory frameworks, he added, should be principles-based, technology-neutral and proportionate to risk, while promoting competition, ensuring non-discriminatory access to underlying infrastructure and improving information symmetry. He also emphasised the need for greater coordination among financial regulators, simpler and more predictable compliance processes, and continued efforts to reduce frictions and interoperability gaps.

Shri Gauba noted the steps taken by the Government to attract long-term domestic and foreign capital, by improving investor confidence in aspects of fair treatment, predictable policy, strong data governance, cybersecurity, and adequate space for innovation.

Concluding his remarks, Shri Gauba said reform has to be an integral part of the culture of governance, supported by long-term and strategic thinking. Prime Minister’s call for Viksit Bharat by 2047 to be approached as a national enterprise, with government, industry and citizens each playing an important role in sustaining India’s reform and growth momentum.

- On fintech, he pointed to India’s digital public infrastructure, including Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, and the account aggregator framework, as globally replicable models built on open, secure, and interoperable infrastructure.
- He said technology-sector regulation should be principles-based, technology-neutral, proportionate to risk, and supportive of competition, non-discriminatory access, and improved information symmetry.
- He emphasized coordination among financial regulators, simpler and more predictable compliance, reduced frictions, and addressing interoperability gaps.
- He noted Government efforts to attract long-term domestic and foreign capital by improving investor confidence through fair treatment, predictable policy, strong data governance, cybersecurity, and space for innovation.
- He concluded that reform should become part of governance culture and that Viksit Bharat by 2047 should be treated as a national enterprise involving government, industry, and citizens.

headline: India–Malaysia Bilateral Meeting
fullText:

India–Malaysia Bilateral Meeting

India Strengthens Agricultural Cooperation with Malaysia, Timor-Leste and Myanmar

Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan Holds Bilateral Talks with Malaysia, Timor-Leste and Myanmar to Deepen Agricultural Partnerships

India Explores New Avenues for Agricultural Research, Innovation, Trade and Food Security with ASEAN Partners

10 SEP 2026 11:04AM by PIB Delhi

A meeting between Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, Union Minister of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India and H.E. Mr. Mohamed Bin Sabu, Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Malaysia was held on 9 September 2026 at New Delhi on the side lines of the 9th ASEAN–India Ministerial Meeting on Agriculture and Forestry (9th AIMMAF) organized by Department of Agricultural Research (DARE)/Indian Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR) at New Delhi during 8–9 September 2026.

The Minister’s noted the importance of sharing knowledge, expertise and best practices, and expressed interest in strengthening collaboration in joint agricultural research, technology and innovation through the mechanism of Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to provide an institutional framework for cooperation in areas of mutual interest in agriculture and allied sectors. Both the Ministers noted that bilateral issues relating to germplasm exchange, trade, and market access could be addressed through mutual cooperation to strengthen the close and strong partnership between India and Malaysia in Agriculture and related issues.

The Indian delegation included Dr M. L. Jat, Secretary, DARE & DG, ICAR; Shri Gyanendra Dev Tripathi, Additional Secretary, DARE & Secretary, ICAR; Shri A. K. Sahu, Joint Secretary (IC), DoAFW; ICAR DDGs; and the International Relations Team led by Dr. Naveen P. Singh, ADG (IR), ICAR.

India–Timor-Leste Bilateral Meeting

A meeting between Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, Union Minister of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India and H.E. Mr. Marcos Da Cruz Minister, Ministry of Agriculture Livestock, Fisheries and Forestry, Timor Leste was held on 9 September 2026 at New Delhi on the side lines of the 9th ASEAN–India Ministerial Meeting on Agriculture and Forestry (9th AIMMAF) organized by Department of Agricultural Research (DARE)/Indian Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR) at New Delhi during 8–9 September 2026.

The Minister from Timor Leste expressed interest on building strong institutional mechanism between both sides to address various challenges in Agriculture and ensuring food security for the nation. Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, Union Minister of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India reiterated the commitment of Government of India to share its best practices to support Timor Leste in advancing their agriculture research and innovation capabilities through exchange of scientists and experts, and human resource development.

The Minister from Timor Leste also expressed interest that India may consider deputing a team of technical and scientific experts to Timor-Leste to assess ground-level challenges and provide technical recommendations in the areas of agriculture, forestry, livestock and aquaculture.

India–Myanmar Bilateral Meeting

A meeting between Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, Union Minister of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India and H.E. Mr. Min Naung, Union Minister, Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Irrigation, Myanmar was held on 9 September 2026 at New Delhi on the side lines of the 9th ASEAN–India Ministerial Meeting on Agriculture and Forestry (9th AIMMAF) organized by Department of Agricultural Research (DARE)/Indian Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR) at New Delhi during 8–9 September 2026.

Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, Union Minister of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Minister, Government of India welcomed the Minister from Myanmar and shared that both sides shared strong cultural and people-to-people connect for a long time and Myanmar is a close partner for India as it share approx. 1600 KM of border with India. The Minister’s noted the that Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the two countries is at an advanced stage of finalisation for strengthening the cooperation in agriculture and allied sectors.

Both sides also discussed the trade potential between two nations and noted that strong partnership between both sides in mutually identified areas will help each other in enhancing the trade in agriculture related goods such as pulses, cotton, dairy development and agriculture education. Myanmar side also suggested favourable investment opportunities in the country to focus on strengthening economic and agricultural ties between the two countries.

10 SEP 2026 10:02AM by PIB Delhi

The Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi, shared a Sanskrit Subhashitam invoking blessings for the well-being, auspiciousness, protection, peace, wisdom and prosperity of all. The Subhashitam seeks the blessings of Lord Indra, Lord Surya, Lord Garuda and Lord Brihaspati.

The Prime Minister shared a Sanskrit Subhashitam-

“स्वस्ति न इन्द्रो वृद्धश्रवाः।

स्वस्ति नः पूषा विश्ववेदाः।

स्वस्ति नस्तार्क्ष्यो अरिष्टनेमिः।

स्वस्ति नो बृहस्पतिर्दधातु॥”

The Subhashitam conveys that May the glorious Lord Indra bless us with well-being. May Lord Surya, the knower of the entire universe and the sustainer of all, bring auspiciousness to us. May Lord Garuda, the destroyer of obstacles, protect us all. May Lord Brihaspati, the lord of knowledge, bless us with peace, wisdom and prosperity.
